page_title: When a Message Uses Fear or Love to Rush You - Digital Confidence Centre
title: When a Message Uses Fear or Love to Rush You
description: How the grandparent scam and other emotional pressure scams work, the 3-Second Rule to pause before acting, how to verify a family emergency, and how to report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. Free, plain-language lesson for Canadian seniors. No account needed.
lesson_time: About 20 minutes, at your own pace
lead: How to recognise when a call is using fear or love to rush you, use the 3-Second Rule to pause before acting, and know exactly who to call to verify, and who to report to.

story.label: Margaret's story
paragraphs: It was a Tuesday afternoon when Margaret's phone rang. The man on the line said he was a police officer and that her grandson David had been in a car accident in Ottawa and was now in jail. "He needs $2,400 for bail and a lawyer right away," the man said. "Please don't tell his parents. It will only make things worse." Margaret's heart was pounding. She loved David. She just wanted to help.

Before we start: the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre receives over 70,000 fraud reports per year. The grandparent scam alone cost Canadians $12.4 million in 2023. You are not alone, and you can learn to spot this.

coach: The hardest part of these scams is that they feel real. A racing heart, a panicking voice, an urgent deadline: these are not signs that the situation is genuine. They are the tools scammers use on purpose. This lesson shows you how to buy back the three seconds your thinking brain needs.

sections.text: Margaret's Tuesday afternoon

The call that came to Margaret that Tuesday was engineered. The caller knew her name. He knew she had a grandson named David. He chose Tuesday afternoon because older adults are more often home and alone mid-week. The grandparent scam is one of the most reported frauds in Canada. Scammers search obituaries, social media, and public records to find grandparents' names, then call pretending to be police, lawyers, or a grandchild in distress.

Three things made the call feel real: urgency ("right away"), authority ("I'm a police officer"), and secrecy ("don't tell his parents"). Every one of those three things is a warning sign, not a reason to act faster.
Margaret did not send money. She said, "I need a moment," and called David on his regular number. He answered immediately from his apartment in Sudbury. He was fine.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: Can you name the three things the scammer used to make the call feel urgent and real? Urgency, authority, and secrecy. When all three show up together, that is a scam signal.
Why fear and love bypass your thinking brain

Your brain has a fast system (emotion, instinct) and a slow system (analysis, judgment). Scammers trigger the fast system on purpose. When you hear "your grandson is in jail," the part of your brain called the amygdala sounds an alarm. Adrenaline floods your body. Your heart beats faster, your hands may shake, and your mind narrows to one thought: help them now.

The prefrontal cortex, the part that normally asks "does this make sense?", is suppressed by adrenaline. This is not a weakness. It is how human brains have always responded to perceived danger. Scammers are professionals at manufacturing that feeling. The solution is not to be smarter or faster. The solution is to buy back three seconds before doing anything. That pause is enough for your slow brain to re-engage.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: True or false: feeling panicked during a scary call means the emergency is real. False. Panic is the tool the scammer is using on you, not evidence that anything has actually happened.
The 3-Second Rule: Stop, Breathe, Verify

The 3-Second Rule is your emergency brake. Any time a call asks you to act immediately out of fear or love, you say: "I need a moment." Then you stop, breathe, and verify through a source you control.

steps.name: Stop
steps.text: Say "I need a moment" out loud. You do not need to explain yourself. You do not owe this caller anything.

steps.name: Breathe
steps.text: Take one slow breath. This is not dramatic; it physically slows your heart rate and lets your thinking brain come back online.

steps.name: Verify
steps.text: Hang up. Call your family member at their regular number, one you already have. Or call a trusted family member who can check. Never use a callback number the caller gives you.

sections.label: The biggest signal
sections.text: If the caller says "you can't hang up or something terrible will happen", that is your biggest signal that something is wrong. Real emergencies can survive a two-minute pause while you verify.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: What are the three steps of the 3-Second Rule? Stop (say "I need a moment"), Breathe (one slow breath), Verify (hang up and call at a number you already have).
The grandparent scam, step by step
Here is the standard script scammers use:

sections.title: How the scam unfolds
steps: The setup call: a person (sometimes pretending to be the grandchild, sometimes an "officer") calls and says there has been an emergency: accident, arrest, or medical crisis. The "grandchild" may be coached to say "Grandma, I need you," then hand the phone to the "officer."
The authority transfer: a second caller takes over as a police officer, lawyer, or court official. They add legal-sounding details: case numbers, court addresses, bail amounts.
The secrecy demand: "Do not tell your son or daughter. It will only make the situation worse. This must be kept confidential." This cuts off your ability to verify with anyone who would question it.
The payment demand: gift cards (iTunes, Google Play, Amazon) or a cash courier who will come to your door. Sometimes wire transfer to a "lawyer's account." These are untraceable, by design.
The urgency escalation: if you hesitate, the caller increases pressure: "He will miss his court date if you don't act now." Real courts do not work this way.

sections.label: The payment signal
sections.text: Gift cards, wire transfers, and cash sent by courier are the only payment methods used in grandparent scams. Real bail, lawyers, and fines are never paid this way. If anyone says "buy gift cards," it is always a scam, full stop.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: What payment type is always a scam signal in the grandparent fraud? Gift cards, along with wire transfers and cash sent by courier. No real court or police force is ever paid that way.
Other emotional pressure patterns
Three rules that never change: the CRA never demands gift cards. Police never demand cash to avoid arrest. You never "win" a prize you did not enter for.

items: CRA imposter scam: a caller claims you owe back taxes and will be arrested within the hour unless you pay by gift card or Interac e-Transfer. The Canada Revenue Agency sends tax notices by mail first. They do not call to demand immediate payment or threaten arrest on a first contact.

Romance scam: a person you met online (often on a dating site or social media) builds a relationship over weeks or months, then reveals a crisis: medical emergency, stuck overseas, business deal gone wrong. Then they ask you to send money. The emotional bond is real; the person is not.

Lottery or prize scam: you receive a call or message that you have won a prize, but must pay a fee, tax, or processing charge first to release the funds. Legitimate lotteries do not require upfront payment. If you did not buy a ticket, you did not win.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: What does the CRA always do first before asking you to pay anything? It sends tax notices by mail. It does not call to demand immediate payment or threaten arrest on a first contact.
How to verify without abandoning someone you love
You are not abandoning your grandchild by hanging up on the caller. You are doing exactly what a loving grandparent would do: checking that it is actually them before acting.

sections.title: The verification steps
steps: Say "I need a moment" and hang up, or just hang up. You do not owe any explanation to a caller who may be a criminal.
Call your family member directly at a number you already have in your phone or address book. Not the number the caller gave you; your own saved number.
If you cannot reach them, call another family member who can check. A sibling, parent, or close friend who might know where they are.
Ask a question only the real person would know. "What did you give me for my birthday last year?" Scammers who have researched you on social media may know basic facts but not personal details.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: When you hang up to verify, what number should you use to call back? The number you already have saved in your phone or address book, never one the caller gives you.
How to report

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC) is run by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP). They want your report even if you recognised the scam and lost nothing. Your report helps them track patterns, issue public warnings, and sometimes identify criminal networks.

sections.label: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre
sections.text: Call 1-888-495-8501 (Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Eastern) or report online at antifraudcentre-centreantifraude.ca. Report even if you did not lose money.

If you lost money, also contact your local police and file a report with your financial institution immediately. Time matters: banks can sometimes reverse wire transfers if reported within hours. If you received a call claiming to be from the CRA, you can also report it directly through the tax fraud reporting page on canada.ca.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: What is the CAFC phone number, and when should you call them? 1-888-495-8501, and you should report every scam attempt, even if no money was lost.
It is not your fault

People who send money to scammers are not gullible. They are people who love their families, who trust authority, and who were targeted by professional criminals using scientifically-designed emotional manipulation. Thousands of Canadians are targeted every year. Many are highly educated.

Shame is the scammer's best tool. If victims feel too embarrassed to report, scammers never get caught. Reporting is an act of protection, for you and for the next person they call. If you or someone you know sent money: report it, do not hide it. The recovery steps (bank, CAFC, police) require a report to begin. Silence only helps the scammer.
Talk to someone you trust. Friends, family, and community members are not going to think less of you for having been targeted. They are more likely to share that it happened to them too.

sections.label: Checkpoint
sections.text: Why do many scam victims not report what happened to them? Shame and embarrassment. But being targeted is not your fault, and reporting is what starts recovery and protects others.
Quick answers

items: What should I do if I get a call saying my grandchild is in jail? Hang up immediately. Then call your grandchild directly at a phone number you already have, not one the caller gives you. Real emergencies can be verified through your family's actual numbers. This is the 3-Second Rule in practice: stop, breathe, and verify through a source you control.

Will real police or the CRA ever call and demand gift cards? No. Never. Real police and the Canada Revenue Agency never demand gift cards, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency as payment. They never threaten immediate arrest on a first phone call. If anyone asks you to buy gift cards to pay a debt or fine, it is always a scam; hang up.

Can I report a scam even if I did not lose any money? Yes, and you should. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC) wants to hear from you even if you hung up immediately. Your report helps the CAFC warn others, identify patterns, and potentially stop the scam from reaching someone else. Call 1-888-495-8501 or report online at antifraudcentre-centreantifraude.ca.

sections.label: The move is
sections.text: Any call that uses fear or love to rush you gets the same answer: "I need a moment." Stop, breathe, and verify at a number you already have. Then report the attempt to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501, even if you lost nothing.

sections.heading: Quick check: test your knowledge
sections.intro: Tap the answer you think is correct. There is no score kept and nothing to sign in to.

questions.q: 1. What is the first step of the 3-Second Rule when you receive a suspicious call?
options: Call a family member right away using the number the caller gives you
STOP: say "I need a moment" and pause before doing anything
Tell the caller you know it is a scam and hang up
Give the caller basic information so the call ends faster
questions.right: Exactly. Stop first: say "I need a moment" out loud. You do not owe the caller any explanation, and that pause lets your thinking brain come back online.
questions.wrong: The first step is STOP: say "I need a moment" and pause. Never use a callback number the caller gives you, and never share information to end the call faster.

questions.q: 2. Why does adrenaline make scam calls more dangerous?
options: It makes you hear more clearly and respond faster
It shuts down the part of your brain that checks facts and judges carefully
It helps you recognise suspicious callers more quickly
It has no real effect on how you think
questions.right: Right. Adrenaline suppresses the prefrontal cortex, the part that asks "does this make sense?" That is exactly why scammers manufacture fear on purpose.
questions.wrong: Adrenaline shuts down the part of your brain that checks facts and judges carefully. That is not a weakness; it is how all human brains respond to perceived danger, and scammers exploit it deliberately.

questions.q: 3. A caller tells you to keep the situation secret from your family. What does this mean?
options: It is a normal police request for confidentiality in active investigations
It is a major red flag: real officers and courts never demand family secrecy
It is protecting your privacy under Canadian law
It is legally required before bail proceedings can begin
questions.right: Correct. The secrecy demand exists to cut off your ability to verify with anyone who would question the story. Real police and courts never demand family secrecy.
questions.wrong: A demand for secrecy is a major red flag. Real officers and courts never demand it; scammers use it to stop you from checking with anyone who would spot the fraud.

questions.q: 4. The CRA will never do which of the following?
options: Send tax notices by mail to your home address
Demand gift cards or threaten immediate arrest on a first phone call
Use automated phone messages for appointment reminders
Contact Canadians by telephone under any circumstances
questions.right: Yes. The Canada Revenue Agency sends tax notices by mail first, and it never demands gift cards or threatens arrest on a first call. Anyone who does is a scammer.
questions.wrong: The CRA will never demand gift cards or threaten immediate arrest on a first phone call. It sends tax notices by mail first. A gift card demand is always a scam.

questions.q: 5. When should you contact the CAFC about a scam?
options: Only if you actually lost money to the scammer
Even if no money was lost: your report helps protect others from the same scam
Only if you know the scammer's real name or location
Only if the amount was over $1,000
questions.right: Exactly. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre wants every report, even when you hung up and lost nothing. Reports help them track patterns and warn others. Call 1-888-495-8501.
questions.wrong: Report every scam attempt, even if no money was lost. The CAFC (1-888-495-8501) uses your report to track patterns, issue warnings, and protect the next person the scammer calls.
